name: Allantoin
lead: Allantoin (5-ureidohydantoin) is a nitrogen-containing compound produced when uric acid is oxidised. Most mammals make it enzymatically; humans do not, and form only small amounts through reactions with reactive oxygen species. It is also found in plants such as comfrey, and cosmetic-grade allantoin is generally synthetic and described as chemically equivalent to the natural form.[1]

It is a long-standing ingredient in over-the-counter skincare, toothpaste, shampoo, lipstick, sun-care and anti-acne products, where it is marketed for moisturising, soothing and skin-smoothing effects.[1]

Clinical research on allantoin is mostly on combination products, particularly scar and wound formulations, so its individual contribution is hard to isolate. No trial in the sources reviewed tests allantoin alone for facial appearance.

paras: Allantoin is a colourless, odourless crystalline powder that dissolves moderately in water (about 0.57 g per 100 mL at 25 C).[1] In animals it arises from oxidation of uric acid during purine breakdown. In most mammals it is the main nitrogen waste in urine, while humans lack the enzyme and its presence in the body is used as a biomarker of oxidative stress.[1]

Cosmetic descriptions credit allantoin with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and moisturising actions, and as a humectant that offsets drying ingredients such as alcohols, sulfates and fragrances.[1] A US DailyMed label lists a topical product containing 0.5 percent allantoin sold as a scar product.[2]

Wikipedia describes the synthetic form as safe, non-toxic and compatible with cosmetic raw materials, citing a cosmetic ingredient safety assessment, and reports a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.[1]

Michele Buniva and Louis Vauquelin first isolated it in 1800, mistakenly believing it came from amniotic fluid; Jean Louis Lassaigne found it in allantoic fluid in 1821, and Wohler and Liebig synthesised it from uric acid in 1837.[1]

Registered trials mostly use allantoin as one ingredient among several. They include a scar study of an onion-extract, allantoin and heparin product (120 participants),[3] an onion-extract and allantoin patch for caesarean scars,[4] a Contractubex scar study after caesarean section,[5] a trial of an allantoin-containing cream in intertrigo compared with hydrocortisone,[6] a cold-sore product study,[7] and early trials in epidermolysis bullosa.[8] Results for these are not summarised in the sources reviewed, and combination designs prevent attributing effects to allantoin alone.
Preclinical reports cited on Wikipedia describe improved insulin resistance in rats and extended lifespan in the worm C. elegans; these are not skin studies.[1]

card.summary: A classic soothing and moisturising additive in drugstore skincare; used in scar and wound combination products, rarely tested on its own.
card.note: Clinical studies are mostly on multi-ingredient products.

quick.overview:
Allantoin is a gentle, widely used skincare ingredient found in moisturisers, scar gels, lip products and sun care. Brands position it as soothing and hydrating.

Studies exist for scar and wound products that contain it, but they combine it with other ingredients, so its own effect is not isolated.
quick.mechanism: Cosmetic sources describe it as a humectant that attracts water and as having mild anti-inflammatory and antioxidant action. Humans do not make it enzymatically.
quick.risks: Described by Wikipedia as safe and non-toxic in cosmetic use, with a rat oral LD50 above 5,000 mg per kg.
